Assess the reasons why Lumora might form a joint venture with a distributor in Belmar. (12 marks)
practice.guidance:
Find the reasons the source actually supports — one of them may leave the firm no real choice — and weigh them against what a joint venture costs. Finish with a judgement on which reason is strongest, and say why.
Level 1: knowledge of what a joint venture is or of general reasons for one. Level 2: application — foreign firms may own no more than 49% of a distribution business, so a legal requirement makes a local partner necessary; a Belmar distributor already reaches the shops, giving access to a distribution network and local knowledge. Level 3: analysis — the partner's network gets cookers onto shelves quickly, which the export plan depends on, and knowledge of the three chains may improve the terms; against that, shared control means shared profit, slower decisions and a partner who may later sell a rival's product. Level 4: evaluation with a supported judgement, for example that the legal requirement is decisive because it removes the alternative of owning distribution outright, so the real question is choosing the right partner.
A strong answer, in outline: the ownership cap makes a partner a legal requirement; the partner also brings a distribution network and local knowledge the firm lacks; the costs are shared control and profit; the legal requirement is the strongest reason because it settles the form, and the other two decide whether the venture succeeds.

practice.question: Source A. Lumora makes rice cookers in Singapore. For three years its home sales have been flat at 400,000 a year at $50 each, and two low-priced importers now share the same supermarket shelves. Its fixed costs are $4.8m a year and each cooker costs $26 in materials, labour and energy. The directors plan to export 200,000 cookers a year to Belmar, where household disposable income is $4,000 and rising 7% a year, three supermarket chains sell most small appliances, and foreign firms may own no more than 49% of a distribution business. They are also choosing a site for a new $20m factory expected to earn $3m a year. Inside the trade bloc that includes Belmar, labour would cost $6 a cooker and freight $1. Outside it, labour would cost $4 and freight $2, cookers entering the bloc pay a 10% tariff, and the government offers a $5m grant. Other costs are $10 a cooker at either site. The exchange rate is $1 = 4 units of Belmar's currency, and engineers and technicians are in short supply in Singapore. Evaluate which of the two sites Lumora should choose for its new factory. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Compare the two sites on the same basis before anything else: what each cooker costs to make and deliver to a customer inside the bloc, and what the firm must invest. Then bring in the factors the source mentions that do not show up in those figures, and finish with a recommendation that says what would change it.
Level 1: describes location factors with little reference to the source. Level 2: knowledge and application — inside the bloc a cooker costs $6 + $10 + $1 = $17 delivered; outside it $14 plus a $1.40 tariff plus $2 freight = $17.40. Level 3: analysis — the cheaper wage is outweighed by the tariff and freight, so the bloc site is $0.40 a cooker cheaper on 200,000 exports; but the grant cuts the outside site's outlay to $15m, lifting the return from 15% to 20% on the same $3m. Level 4: evaluation — weighs a one-off grant against a cost gap that lasts the life of the factory, considers skills, infrastructure and stability not given in the source, and reaches a perceptive recommendation with conditions.
A strong answer, in outline: the bloc site wins on delivered cost; the grant makes the other site's return look better but only for as long as the tariff gap does not erode the $3m forecast; recommend the bloc site, unless the grant is large enough, or the firm's sales outside the bloc large enough, that the tariff matters less.

practice.question: Source A. Lumora makes rice cookers in Singapore. For three years its home sales have been flat at 400,000 a year at $50 each, and two low-priced importers now share the same supermarket shelves. Its fixed costs are $4.8m a year and each cooker costs $26 in materials, labour and energy. The directors plan to export 200,000 cookers a year to Belmar, where household disposable income is $4,000 and rising 7% a year, three supermarket chains sell most small appliances, and foreign firms may own no more than 49% of a distribution business. They are also choosing a site for a new $20m factory expected to earn $3m a year. Inside the trade bloc that includes Belmar, labour would cost $6 a cooker and freight $1. Outside it, labour would cost $4 and freight $2, cookers entering the bloc pay a 10% tariff, and the government offers a $5m grant. Other costs are $10 a cooker at either site. The exchange rate is $1 = 4 units of Belmar's currency, and engineers and technicians are in short supply in Singapore. Evaluate whether exchange rate movements or skill shortages pose the greater threat to Lumora's international competitiveness. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
Treat competitiveness as having two sides — price and non-price — and ask which threat damages which side, and for how long. Use the source to judge how exposed this firm is to each, then reach a conclusion that says what would make you change it.
Level 1: describes exchange rates or skill shortages in general terms. Level 2: knowledge and application — an appreciation to $1 = 5 units would take a $50 cooker from 200 units to 250 units in Belmar; the shortage of engineers and technicians raises wages and can delay new models. Level 3: analysis of both — the currency affects price competitiveness on every export and can reverse; the skill shortage raises costs and weakens non-price competitiveness (quality, new designs) for as long as it lasts, and affects home sales too. Level 4: evaluation — judges which is greater for this firm, for example that the exchange rate is the larger short-run threat to an exporter competing on price with powerful buyers, while the skill shortage is the more lasting threat, especially if the factory is built at home; the conclusion states the condition that would change it.
A strong answer, in outline: the exchange rate hits price competitiveness quickly and can be managed by producing inside the bloc; the skill shortage hits both price and quality and cannot be hedged; so the skill shortage is the greater long-term threat unless the new factory is built abroad, where the currency becomes the larger risk.

flashcards.front: What is a push factor?
flashcards.back: A condition in the home market that drives a firm abroad. The two named here are a saturated market and competition.

flashcards.front: What is a saturated market?
flashcards.back: A market where most people who want the product already have it, so sales can grow only by replacement or by taking customers from rivals.

flashcards.front: How is competition a push factor?
flashcards.back: Rivals at home take share and force prices down, so growing abroad, away from the same rivals, becomes more attractive.

flashcards.front: What is a pull factor?
flashcards.back: An opportunity abroad that draws a firm in: increased sales and profitability, risk spreading and economies of scale.

flashcards.front: How does selling abroad spread risk?
flashcards.back: Sales no longer depend on one economy. A downturn at home hits only part of total sales if other markets hold up.

flashcards.front: Why does exporting lower average cost at home too?
flashcards.back: Fixed costs are spread over all units made, so a larger output lowers the cost of every unit, including those sold at home.

flashcards.front: Off-shoring or outsourcing: what is the difference?
flashcards.back: Off-shoring is WHERE — the activity moves to another country. Outsourcing is WHO — another firm does it. A firm can do both at once.

flashcards.front: What is cost competitiveness?
flashcards.back: The ability to produce at a cost that lets a firm match or beat rivals' prices; off-shoring and outsourcing are two routes to it.

flashcards.front: How does selling abroad extend the product life cycle?
flashcards.back: A product declining at home can be at an early stage in a market where few people own it yet, so its sales last longer.

flashcards.front: Name the five factors for assessing a country as a market.
flashcards.back: Levels and growth of disposable income; ease of doing business; infrastructure; political stability; exchange rates.

flashcards.front: Why do both the level and the growth of income matter?
flashcards.back: The level says who can afford the product now; the growth says how many more will be able to soon.

flashcards.front: What is ease of doing business?
flashcards.back: The time and cost of trading legally in a country: permits, registration, enforcing contracts and getting paid.

flashcards.front: What are Porter's five forces?
flashcards.back: Rivalry among existing firms, threat of new entrants, buyer power, supplier power and threat of substitutes.

flashcards.front: How are the five forces used to assess a potential market?
flashcards.back: Rate each force for that market; strong forces mean the profit a newcomer can expect is low, whatever the market's size.

flashcards.front: Name the nine factors for assessing a production location.
flashcards.back: Costs of production; skills and availability of labour force; infrastructure; location in trade bloc; government incentives; ease of doing business; political stability; natural resources; likely return on investment.

flashcards.front: Why can a low-wage site be the dearer one?
flashcards.back: Delivered cost per unit includes tariffs and freight. A tariff on goods entering a bloc can cost more than the wage gap saves.

flashcards.front: Why does location inside a trade bloc matter?
flashcards.back: Goods made inside move to other members without the common external tariff that goods from outside pay.

flashcards.front: What government incentives attract a factory?
flashcards.back: Grants, tax holidays, cheap land and special economic zones. They can end, and some carry conditions.

flashcards.front: How is return on investment calculated?
flashcards.back: Annual return ÷ the money invested × 100. A grant raises it by reducing the money the firm puts in.

flashcards.front: Merger, takeover or joint venture?
flashcards.back: Merger: two firms become one. Takeover: one firm controls another. Joint venture: partners create a new business they own together.

flashcards.front: Name the ten reasons for global mergers, takeovers or joint ventures.
flashcards.back: Spreading risk and economies of scale; new markets/trade blocs; brands/patents; resources/supplies; global competitiveness; reducing competition; local knowledge; government or legal requirement; supply chains/distribution networks; sharing costs/risks.

flashcards.front: When is a joint venture a legal requirement?
flashcards.back: When a country limits foreign ownership in an industry or requires a local partner, so no other route is allowed.

flashcards.front: What does a distribution network give a buyer?
flashcards.back: Established links to wholesalers, retailers and delivery routes that get the product to customers without years of building them.

flashcards.front: What does an appreciation of the home currency do to an exporter?
flashcards.back: Its price abroad rises if it holds its home price, or its home-currency receipt falls if it holds the foreign price.

flashcards.front: What does an appreciation do to an importer?
flashcards.back: Imported inputs cost less in the home currency, so its costs fall.

flashcards.front: Why does repatriated profit change with the exchange rate?
flashcards.back: Profit earned in a foreign currency is worth fewer home-currency units when the home currency is stronger.

flashcards.front: How can a firm reduce exchange rate risk?
flashcards.back: Buy inputs in the currency it earns, produce inside the market, agree a rate in advance with a bank, or invoice in its own currency.

flashcards.front: What is international competitiveness?
flashcards.back: The ability to win sales against foreign rivals, on price (cost) or on non-price factors such as quality, design and service.

flashcards.front: How do skill shortages affect international competitiveness?
flashcards.back: Scarce skills raise wages and leave posts unfilled, lifting costs and delaying products, which weakens both price and non-price competitiveness.

mistakes.title: Calling every reason to go abroad a push factor
mistakes.mistake: Writing that rising incomes in the target country "push" the firm to export.
mistakes.correction: A push factor is a problem at home (a saturated market, competition); an attraction abroad (sales, profit, scale, risk spreading) is a pull factor. Many decisions have both.
mistakes.examTip: Label each reason push or pull before developing it; the label tells you where the evidence should come from.

mistakes.title: Treating off-shoring and outsourcing as the same thing
mistakes.mistake: Describing a firm that builds its own factory abroad as having "outsourced" production.
mistakes.correction: Off-shoring is about location; outsourcing is about ownership. The firm running its own foreign factory has off-shored but not outsourced.
mistakes.examTip: Ask two questions of the case: where is the work done, and who does it?

mistakes.title: Comparing wages instead of delivered cost
mistakes.mistake: Choosing the site with the lowest wage as the cheapest place to produce.
mistakes.correction: Delivered cost per unit adds materials, energy, freight and any tariff. A tariff on goods entering a trade bloc can outweigh a lower wage.
mistakes.examTip: Add every cost line the case gives into one figure per unit for each site before comparing.

mistakes.title: Listing the five forces without rating them
mistakes.mistake: Naming rivalry, entrants, buyers, suppliers and substitutes, then moving on.
mistakes.correction: The forces only assess a market when each is rated for that market and the ratings lead to a conclusion about likely profit.
mistakes.examTip: Pick the forces the case gives evidence for, rate each high or low, and say what they imply for price.

mistakes.title: Calling every cross-border deal a merger
mistakes.mistake: Describing a firm buying a majority of a rival's shares as a merger.
mistakes.correction: That is a takeover. A merger is agreed and creates one combined firm; a joint venture creates a new business both partners own while they carry on separately.
mistakes.examTip: Identify which of the three the case describes before giving reasons, because the reasons differ.

mistakes.title: Reading a strong currency as good news for every firm
mistakes.mistake: Writing that an appreciation "strengthens" a firm, whatever it does.
mistakes.correction: An appreciation hurts exporters (dearer abroad or lower receipts) and helps importers (cheaper inputs). A firm that does both must net the two.
mistakes.examTip: Work out the export effect and the import effect with the figures given, then judge the net impact.

mistakes.title: Treating skill shortages only as a wage problem
mistakes.mistake: Saying a shortage of engineers raises costs, and stopping there.
mistakes.correction: Shortages also delay products and lower quality, which weakens non-price competitiveness — often the more lasting damage.
mistakes.examTip: Follow the shortage to both price and non-price competitiveness, and weigh the firm's options for closing the gap.

chains.title: Extending a product's life cycle abroad
steps: Customers at home move to newer models, and sales of the product there begin to fall.
The firm looks for a country where few households own the product yet.
It launches the same model there, and sales abroad grow.
Growth abroad offsets decline at home, so the model sells for years longer.
chains.result: The product is unchanged; the market is new. The extra years earn a margin on development costs that were paid long ago.

chains.title: From an export plan to a lower average cost
steps: Lumora adds 200,000 exports to 400,000 home sales.
Fixed costs of $4.8m are now shared by 600,000 cookers instead of 400,000.
Fixed cost per cooker falls from $12 to $8, so average cost falls from $38 to $34.
Every cooker, including those sold at home, is now cheaper to make.
chains.result: Economies of scale are a pull factor that also strengthens the firm at home.

chains.title: Working out the likely return on a new factory
steps: Estimate the yearly profit the factory should earn: $3m.
Take any grant off the cost of building it: $20m less $5m is $15m.
Divide the yearly profit by the firm's own money: 20%, against 15% with no grant.
Weigh that percentage against the chance it is not earned in that country.
chains.result: Return on investment is where the location factors meet; its reliability depends on the ones that are hardest to put a figure on.

chains.title: From a stronger dollar to lost export sales
steps: The dollar rises from $1 = 4 units to $1 = 5 units.
A cooker still priced at $50 now costs buyers abroad 250 units of their currency, not 200 units.
Customers in Belmar switch to cheaper local cookers.
The exporter sells fewer units there — or holds the local price and earns $40 a cooker instead.
chains.result: An appreciation costs an exporter volume or margin; the same movement makes its imported parts cheaper.

evaluation.title: Which market: the richer one or the faster-growing one?
evaluation.content: A richer market is not automatically the better one. Tarsia's households have $9,000 to spend against Belmar's $4,000, but Belmar's incomes are growing 7% a year against 1%. Three things decide it. THE PRODUCT: an affordable, basic cooker suits the market where incomes are crossing the point at which it becomes affordable; a premium model suits the richer one. THE FORCES: a large market with three dominant retailers can leave less profit than a smaller one with many outlets. THE RISKS: fast growth is worth less if the rules, the infrastructure or the currency cannot be relied on. The strongest conclusion names the product and the force that decide it.

evaluation.title: Merger, takeover or joint venture?
evaluation.content: The three routes trade control against cost and risk. A takeover gives full control of brands, patents and networks, and costs the most. A merger shares ownership but still combines the firms entirely. A joint venture shares the cost and the risk, brings the partner's local knowledge and networks, and is sometimes the only legal route — at the price of shared profit and slower decisions. The deciding question is what the firm needs: to own an asset outright, or to use it in one market.

evaluation.title: Is a stronger home currency a threat?
evaluation.content: It depends on which side of the firm is larger. Lumora's exports would cost 250 units instead of 200 units after a 25% appreciation, but a part invoiced at 60 units would fall from $15 to $12. A firm that exports much and imports little loses; one that imports most of its inputs may gain. Producing inside the market it sells to, or buying in the currency it earns, shrinks the question.
